big: Imagine a fund that sells some of its equity when prices look rich and buys more when they look cheap, without anyone deciding it on the day. That is a balanced advantage fund.

lines: Does this fund protect me when markets fall?
It tries to, in a particular way. Watch what its equity dial does, then what that cost and gained in a made-up decade.

alt: Three bars showing a balanced advantage fund holding less equity as markets get expensive
caps: A model reads how expensive the market is, often by its price to earnings ratio.
When markets look cheap, net equity goes up. Here it is 70%.
When they look fair, the dial sits in the middle. Here it is 50%.
When markets look expensive, the fund cuts net equity. Here it is 30%. The numbers are an illustration.
It cuts equity by hedging with futures, so the fund keeps its equity-style tax status.

h: Smoother, not safe: a made-up decade
alt: Two lines showing a balanced advantage fund falling less than an equity fund in a bad year but lagging in a strong rally
caps: Made-up paths. The equity fund and the dial fund start together at ₹100.
Year 3: equity falls hard. The dial fund had cut equity, so it dips only about 8%.
Years 7 and 8: a strong rally. The dial fund holds back at high prices and gains less.
Deepest falls: equity -26%, dial fund -8%. The equity fund still ends higher.
A smoother ride bought with a lower finish. Neither path is a promise.

h: What the dial can and cannot do
title: Fair claims, and unfair ones
stops: Cuts equity when valuations are high
Falls are often smaller than in equity funds
alt: A shield with true and false claims about balanced advantage funds
caps: It trims equity when valuations are high, so falls are often smaller than in a pure equity fund.
It does not remove losses, and in a strong rally it can trail an equity fund.
So compare funds by their model, how often it changes and how they behaved in 2020.

q: The market's price to earnings ratio rises from 20 to 28, and a balanced advantage fund's model cuts net equity from 50% to 30%. What is the likely effect on a client over the next two years?
opts: Larger falls if prices drop, since cutting equity locks in a return
No change either way, since the tax status keeps its return fixed
Smaller falls if prices drop, but a lag if the rally continues
Higher returns in a rally, since selling equity high adds gains
why: Cutting equity lowers exposure to a fall. Nothing about the move locks in a fixed return for the fund.
Tax status does not fix returns. The equity share changed, so the fund's ups and downs change with it.
With less equity, a fall hurts less. If prices keep rising, the lower equity share earns less than a full equity fund.
Selling early can miss further gains. In a rally that keeps going, the fund with less equity trails.

q: In the made-up decade, the dial fund fell about 8% in year 3 but gained only about 18% in each of the two big rally years, while equity gained 28% and 35%. A client says the fund is the weaker one. What is the best reply?
opts: Agree, since lagging in a rally shows the model has totally failed
It lagged only because the fund charges more when markets rise
Ignore the rally years, since only the worst year counts
Its job is a smoother ride, so judge it across the whole cycle
why: Lagging in a rally is expected for this type, so one rally year is not proof of a broken model.
A fund's expense ratio is a fixed yearly percentage. It does not rise with the market.
Both the fall and the rally years matter. Choosing only one year would give a false picture.
Holding back at high prices is the design. The cost shows in the rally and the benefit shows in the fall.

q: Rohan is choosing between two balanced advantage funds. Which comparison is most useful?
opts: Each fund's last one-year return, since it shows the better model
Each model, how often it shifts equity, and its 2020 record
The fund house's brand, since big houses build better models
The number of units in each fund, since more units show more skill
why: A one-year return reflects one market's mood. It says little about whether the model works through a cycle.
The model and its record in a hard year show how the fund tries to protect. That is what the category promises.
A big name does not show how a model reads valuations. Two funds in one house can differ.
The number of units reflects a fund's unit price and size, not the skill of its model.

q: A balanced advantage fund cuts its net equity to 30% by selling futures against the shares it holds. A client asks if it will now be taxed like a debt fund. What is correct?
opts: Yes, the net equity of 30% is below 35%, so slab-rate tax applies
It depends on the client's slab, which fixes the fund's tax status
Hedging keeps gross equity high, so it stays equity-like for tax
It becomes tax-exempt, since hedged equity does not count as equity
why: The equity share used for tax counts the shares held, not the net level after futures hedges.
A fund's tax category depends on what it holds. The client's slab changes the rate, not the category.
Futures hedges cut the net level while shares stay held, so the fund can keep its equity-style tax status.
Hedged equity is still equity-related and does not give the fund a tax exemption.

pts: Net equity moves with valuations: down when markets are dear, up when cheap.
Smoother, not safe. Falls are often smaller and rallies can be lagged.
Compare funds on their model, how it behaved in 2020, and its record.
